parts.prompt_html: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\).
parts.solution_html:
Subtract the position vector of A from those of B and C, then calculate

\[\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}3\\-3\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}10\\10\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: Find the value of \(t\) for which \(A,B,C,D\) are coplanar.
parts.solution_html:
The non-zero vector product gives a normal to plane ABC. Thus D is in this plane exactly when

\[\overrightarrow{AD}\cdot\mathbf n=0\]
\[2 \left(t - 3\right)=0\]
\[t=3\]

The non-zero normal also confirms that A, B and C are not collinear.

stem_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\1\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

parts.prompt_html: The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.
parts.solution_html:
Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6\\- 3 \lambda + \mu + 3\\3 - 2 \lambda\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 17 \lambda + 5 \mu + 27=0\]
\[- 5 \lambda + 2 \mu + 9=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.
parts.hint_html: Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

parts.prompt_html: Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.
parts.solution_html:
The joining direction is \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), perpendicular to both line directions. Using the foot \(\left(2,-3,0\right)\) gives

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Substitution of the second foot confirms that it lies on the same line.

parts.prompt_html: Show that \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew, and find their exact shortest distance.
parts.solution_html:
A common perpendicular direction is

\[\mathbf n=\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]

Project the connector between the two given anchors onto this normal:

\[d=\frac{|(\mathbf b-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-58|}{\sqrt{29}}=2 \sqrt{29}\]

The vector product is non-zero and the scalar product is non-zero, so the lines are non-parallel and non-coplanar: they are skew.

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 13 \lambda + 7 \mu + 40=0\]
\[- 7 \lambda + 6 \mu + 26=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=2,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\4\\11\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\6\\8\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

parts.prompt_html: Find the shortest distance between \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) as a function of \(t\).
parts.solution_html:
The line directions have vector product

\[\mathbf n(t)=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1 - t\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

This vector never vanishes. The anchor connector has scalar product \(- t - 3\) with it, so the perpendicular separation is

\[d(t)=\frac{|- t - 3|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}\]

A zero numerator corresponds to intersecting, not skew, lines; the same expression then gives distance zero.

parts.prompt_html: Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\).
parts.solution_html:
Use the distance expression obtained above.

\[\frac{|- t - 3|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 2 t + 3}}=\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[- \frac{2 \left(t - 4\right) \left(19 t - 6\right)}{11}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{6}{19}\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{7 \sqrt{11}}{11}\). Both values are admissible.

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}t^{2} - 5 t + 7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

\[x + 3 y - z=-2\]

parts.prompt_html: Classify the position of \(l_t\) relative to \(\Pi\) for every real \(t\).
parts.answer_html: \(t=1\): the entire line lies in \(\Pi\). \(t=4\): parallel and disjoint. All other real values: a unique intersection.
parts.solution_html:
Substitution into the plane equation gives

\[\left(t - 1\right) \left(\lambda t - 4 \lambda + 1\right)=0\]

If \(t=1\), this is true for every \(\lambda\), so the line is contained. If \(t=4\), the left side is the non-zero constant \(3\), so there is no intersection. Otherwise it gives exactly one value of \(\lambda\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(X\), the point where \(l_t\) meets \(\Pi\).

\[3+(10)\lambda=-2\]
\[\lambda=- \frac{1}{2}\]

Since \(10\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{1}{2}\\\frac{1}{2}\\3\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: Find the acute angle between \(l_t\) and \(\Pi\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}13\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|10|}{\sqrt{1870}}=\frac{\sqrt{1870}}{187}\]
\[\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{1870}}{187}\right)=13.4^\circ\]

parts.prompt_html: Find the position vector of \(H\), the foot of the perpendicular from \(P\) to the plane. Hence find the reflection \(R\) of \(P\) in the plane.
parts.solution_html:
The perpendicular has direction \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\5\\2\end{pmatrix}\), so write \(\mathbf h=\mathbf p-\tau\mathbf n\). Substituting into the plane equation gives

\[121-65\tau=-9\]
\[\tau=2\]

Therefore

\[\overrightarrow{OH}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\5\end{pmatrix}\]

The foot is the midpoint of the original point and its reflection:

\[\mathbf r=2\mathbf h-\mathbf p=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: Find a vector equation of the reflection of \(l\) in the plane, explaining how its direction is obtained.
parts.solution_html:
For any point \(\mathbf x\), its reflection in the plane is

\[\mathbf x^*=\mathbf x-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Insert \(\mathbf x=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) and collect the constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf p^*=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf w}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-7\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence the image line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-16\\-9\\1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-7\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.
parts.solution_html:
Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- \lambda + \mu - 3\\2 \lambda - \mu + 8\\- 3 \lambda + \mu - 7\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 2 \left(7 \lambda - 3 \mu + 20\right)=0\]
\[- 3 \left(2 \lambda - \mu + 6\right)=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=-2,\qquad\mu=2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\3\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

parts.prompt_html: Find the equation of \(\Pi\) and explain why its points are equidistant from \(P\) and \(Q\).

A normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\), and the midpoint of \(PQ\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{3}{2}\\3\\\frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}\). Thus the plane is

\[x + 2 y + z=11\]

Expanding \(|\mathbf r-\mathbf p|^2=|\mathbf r-\mathbf q|^2\) gives the same equation, so every point of this plane is equidistant from \(P,Q\).

parts.prompt_html: Find the two planes parallel to \(\Pi\) that contain \(l_1\) and \(l_2\), respectively. Find their perpendicular separation.

\[\frac{|6|}{\sqrt{6}}=\sqrt{6}\]

A normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), and the midpoint of \(PQ\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\\frac{9}{2}\\\frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}\). Thus the plane is

\[y - z=1\]

Expanding \(|\mathbf r-\mathbf p|^2=|\mathbf r-\mathbf q|^2\) gives the same equation, so every point of this plane is equidistant from \(P,Q\).
parts.hint_html: Use the midpoint as an anchor and PQ as a normal; expand the squared distances for the justification.

parts.prompt_html: Find a vector equation of the reflection of \(l_1\) in the plane, explaining how its direction is obtained.
parts.solution_html:
For any point \(\mathbf x\), its reflection in the plane is

\[\mathbf x^*=\mathbf x-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf x-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Insert \(\mathbf x=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) and collect the constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf p^*=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\mathbf w^*=\mathbf w-2\frac{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf w}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence the image line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Reflect a general point on the line, not only the anchor.

criteria.criterion_html: Reflect the anchor using its perpendicular foot.
Reflect the direction, reversing its normal component.

parts.prompt_html: Determine whether the reflected image of \(l_1\) intersects \(l_2\). Justify your answer.
parts.solution_html: Reflection sends \(P\) to \(Q\) and leaves the direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) unchanged, since it is parallel to the mirror plane. The image line therefore passes through \(Q\). Its direction is not parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), so the intersection is unique.
parts.hint_html: Track the reflected foot and compare the two directions.

criteria.criterion_html: Show the reflected first foot is Q.
Show non-parallel directions, hence a unique intersection.

For each real \(t\), a line \(l_t\) has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}t - 3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}t^{2} - 3 t + 3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

The fixed plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[x + 3 y - z=-2\]

parts.prompt_html: Classify the position of \(l_t\) relative to \(\Pi\) for every real \(t\).
parts.answer_html: \(t=0\): the entire line lies in \(\Pi\). \(t=3\): parallel and disjoint. All other real values: a unique intersection.
parts.solution_html:
Substitution into the plane equation gives

\[t \left(\lambda t - 3 \lambda + 1\right)=0\]

If \(t=0\), this is true for every \(\lambda\), so the line is contained. If \(t=3\), the left side is the non-zero constant \(3\), so there is no intersection. Otherwise it gives exactly one value of \(\lambda\).

criteria.criterion_html: Substitute the line into the plane equation.

parts.prompt_html: Find the unique intersection in terms of \(t\), stating the parameter restrictions.
parts.solution_html:
For \(t\ne 0,3\), division is valid. Thus \(\lambda=-1/(t-3)\). Inserting it into the line cancels the component in \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and leaves

\[\mathbf x=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}-\frac1{t-3}\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: Describe exactly the locus of the unique intersection points, including any omitted points.

Plane \(\Pi_2\) has equation \(5 x + y=7\). A point \(P\) and line direction \(\mathbf w\) are defined by

The constants \(a\) and \(b\) are positive.

parts.prompt_html: Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_1\).
parts.solution_html:
Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}=7\]

Using the point \(\left(-1,2,3\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x + 2 y + 2 z=7\]

parts.prompt_html: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).
parts.solution_html:
A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\10\\-7\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-10\\7\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(1,2,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[7=7,\qquad 7=7\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-10\\7\end{pmatrix}\]

\[\operatorname{dist}(P,\Pi_1)=|a-3|\sqrt{17}\]

Equating this to \(\sqrt{17}\) gives \(a=2\text{ or }a=4\). Retain only the positive values:

\[a=2\quad\text{or}\quad4\]

parts.prompt_html: The line through \(P\) in direction \(\mathbf w\) makes an acute angle of 45° with \(\Pi_1\). Find \(b\) exactly.
parts.solution_html:
Since \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n=0\), the line direction has squared length \(17 b^{2} + 9\). For a 45° line–plane angle,

\[\frac{b|\mathbf n|}{\sqrt{|\mathbf u|^2+b^2|\mathbf n|^2}}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\]

Squaring and simplifying gives \(17 b^{2}\)=\(9\). Positivity selects

\[b=\frac{3 \sqrt{17}}{17}\]

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{11}{7}\\- \frac{34}{21}\\3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{5 \sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.

The plane \(\Pi\) has equation

\[3 x + y + z=-11\]

Line \(l\) passes through \(P=\left(2,-1,6\right)\) and has equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\6\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

The orthogonal projection of \(l\) onto \(\Pi\) is the locus of the perpendicular feet of all points of \(l\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(X\), the point where \(l\) meets \(\Pi\).
parts.solution_html:
Substitute the line into the plane equation:

\[11+(11)\lambda=-11\]
\[\lambda=-2\]

Since \(11\)\(\ne0\), there is exactly one intersection. Substitution into the line gives

\[\overrightarrow{OX}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-1\\8\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: State a normal \(\mathbf n\) to the plane and calculate \(\mathbf n\times\mathbf w\), where \(\mathbf w\) is the line direction.
parts.solution_html:
Read the normal from the plane equation and evaluate the component vector product:

\[\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}4\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\7\\-4\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: The coefficients of x, y, z form a plane normal.

parts.prompt_html: Find a vector equation of the orthogonal projection of \(l\) onto \(\Pi\).
parts.solution_html:
Project a general point \(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w\) onto the plane. Removing the normal component gives

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w-\frac{\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf p+\lambda\mathbf w)-d}{\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf n}\mathbf n\]

Collect constant and parameter terms:

\[\mathbf h(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\]

The new direction is non-zero and has zero dot product with \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Thus this is a line in the plane, not a single point. Equivalently, a direction is \((\mathbf n\times\mathbf w)\times\mathbf n\).

stem_html:
The line \(l_1\) has vector equation

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-6\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

A second line \(l_2\) is given by

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}8\\-3\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

All line parameters are real.

Let \(A\) and \(B\) be the given anchors on \(l_1\) and \(l_2\). The common perpendicular meets them at \(P\) and \(Q\), respectively.

parts.prompt_html: The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors.
parts.solution_html:
Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}\mu + 9\\- 2 \lambda + \mu + 3\\- \lambda - 3 \mu - 3\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 5 \lambda - \mu + 3=0\]
\[\lambda + 11 \mu + 21=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=1,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-4\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-5\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.
parts.hint_html: Use two independent parameters and require the joining vector to have zero dot product with both directions.

parts.prompt_html: Find the exact area of triangle \(APQ\).
parts.solution_html:
The two side vectors from \(A\) are \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}7\\1\\3\end{pmatrix}\). Their vector product is

\[\overrightarrow{AP}\times\overrightarrow{AQ}=\begin{pmatrix}5\\7\\-14\end{pmatrix}\]

Its magnitude is the area of the parallelogram, so the triangle has half this area:

\[\operatorname{Area}(APQ)=\frac{3 \sqrt{30}}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: Use half the magnitude of the vector product of two sides from the same vertex.

parts.prompt_html: Find the exact volume of tetrahedron \(APQB\). You may use \(V=\frac13\times\text{base area}\times\text{perpendicular height}\).
parts.solution_html:
Take \(APQ\) as the base. Its area is \(\frac{3 \sqrt{30}}{2}\). The perpendicular height is the distance from \(B\) to that plane:

\[h=\frac{6 \sqrt{30}}{5}\]

Using the formula given in the question,

\[V=\frac13\times \frac{3 \sqrt{30}}{2}\times \frac{6 \sqrt{30}}{5}=18\]

parts.prompt_html: The points \(P\in l_1\) and \(Q\in l_2\) are such that \(PQ\) is perpendicular to both lines. Find their position vectors. Hence give a vector equation of the common perpendicular.
parts.solution_html:
Take arbitrary points on the two lines. The connecting vector is

\[\overrightarrow{PQ}=\begin{pmatrix}- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6\\6 - \lambda\\- 2 \left(\lambda - 1\right)\end{pmatrix}\]

Its scalar product with each line direction must vanish:

\[- 9 \lambda + 2 \mu + 22=0\]
\[- 2 \lambda + \mu + 6=0\]

Solving these two equations gives

\[\lambda=2,\qquad\mu=-2\]

Substitute back into the original line equations:

\[\overrightarrow{OP}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\overrightarrow{OQ}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\3\\-3\end{pmatrix}\]

The connector is \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), which has zero dot product with each direction.

A line through \(P\) parallel to \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) is therefore

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\]

parts.prompt_html: Find all real values of \(t\) for which the shortest distance is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).
parts.solution_html:
The common normal is \(\begin{pmatrix}t - 2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\), so the distance formula gives

\[\frac{|2 - 3 t|}{\sqrt{t^{2} - 4 t + 6}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\]

Both sides are non-negative and the denominator is strictly positive, so squaring introduces no additional sign condition:

\[\frac{2 \left(t - 1\right) \left(13 t - 3\right)}{3}=0\]

Solving gives

\[t=\frac{3}{13}\quad\text{or}\quad1\]

Substitution of each value in the original distance formula gives \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). Both values are admissible.

Use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}5\\4\\-4\end{pmatrix}\) and point \(\left(0,0,0\right)\).

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-4\\-2\end{pmatrix}+s\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

The parameters \(s\) and \(t\) are real.

A second plane \(\Pi_2\) has equation

\[3 x - y + z=-5\]

parts.prompt_html: Find a Cartesian equation of \(\Pi_1\).
parts.solution_html:
Two non-parallel directions in the plane are \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\). A normal is their vector product:

\[\mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}=-5\]

Using the point \(\left(-3,-4,-2\right)\) gives the Cartesian equation

\[3 x - y=-5\]
parts.hint_html: Take the vector product of two independent directions, then use a point of the plane.

criteria.criterion_html: Form two directions and their vector product.
Substitute a known point to obtain the constant.

parts.prompt_html: Find the acute angle between \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\), giving your answer in degrees to 1 decimal place.
parts.solution_html:
Use the following normals to the two planes:

\[\mathbf u=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbf n=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Use the acute angle between the two normal vectors. The absolute value removes the arbitrary choice of normal direction.

\[\cos\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|10|}{\sqrt{110}}=\frac{\sqrt{110}}{11}\]
\[\alpha=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{110}}{11}\right)=17.5^\circ\]
parts.hint_html: Use the absolute dot product; use sine for a line–plane angle and cosine for a plane–plane angle.

parts.prompt_html: Find a vector equation of the line of intersection of \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).
parts.solution_html:
A direction of the intersection is perpendicular to both normals:

\[\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Hence we may take direction \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\). Solving the two plane equations with a convenient coordinate set to zero gives the point \(\left(- \frac{5}{3},0,0\right)\). It satisfies both equations:

\[-5=-5,\qquad -5=-5\]

The required line is

\[\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}- \frac{5}{3}\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

criteria.criterion_html: Use the cross product of the normals.
Find a point common to the planes.

We may use the proportional normal \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\). For any point \(\mathbf r\) of the plane, \((\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf n=0\).

\[\mathbf r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=-6\]

The angle between a line and a plane is the complement of the angle between its direction and the plane normal. Therefore use sine, not cosine.

\[\sin\alpha=\frac{|\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf u|\,|\mathbf n|}=\frac{|-3|}{3 \sqrt{7}}=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{7}\]

Relative to the origin \(O\), the points have position vectors

\[\overrightarrow{OA}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

The volume of a tetrahedron is \(\frac13\times\text{base area}\times\text{perpendicular height}\).

parts.prompt_html: Find \(\overrightarrow{OA}\times\overrightarrow{OB}\).
parts.solution_html: \[\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\]
parts.hint_html: Calculate the three components of the vector product.

parts.prompt_html: Deduce the exact area of triangle \(OAB\).
parts.solution_html: \[\text{Area}=\tfrac12|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=\tfrac12\sqrt{81}=\frac{9}{2}\]
parts.hint_html: The vector product gives twice the triangle area.

parts.prompt_html: Find the exact volume of tetrahedron \(OABC\).
parts.solution_html:
Plane OAB has normal \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}\). Its distance from C is

\[h=12/9=\frac{4}{3}\]
\[V=\tfrac13\times\frac{9}{2}\times\frac{4}{3}=2\]
parts.hint_html: Use OAB as the base and the normal component of OC as the height.
